readerTitle: Why "just 1% of a huge market" is the wrong math
caseNote: 가상 사례 (글루텐프리 베이커리, 회계 소프트웨어 회사의 사내 팀) + 투자자들이 흔히 지적하는 '1% 논리' 피칭 패턴 (일반적 관찰) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 시장 규모는 큰 숫자를 잘라서 구하는 것이 아니라, 실제로 닿을 수 있는 고객 한 명 한 명을 세어 쌓아 올려서 구한다.
misconception: 시장이 충분히 크면 1%만 가져와도 큰 사업이 된다.

sources.text: 하향식(top-down)·상향식(bottom-up) 시장 규모 추정은 창업·마케팅 교육의 표준 개념

factChecks.note: '1% 논리'를 투자자들이 경계한다는 내용은 특정 인물·연구를 인용하지 않고 일반적 관찰로만 썼습니다. 통계나 인용을 추가하지 마세요.
TAM/SAM/SOM 용어는 업계에서 흔히 쓰는 약어로만 소개했고, 정의는 일반적인 의미로 단순화했습니다.

cards.title: Why "just 1% of a huge market" is the wrong math
body: A baker's business plan opens with one big number: the country spends $2 billion a year on gluten-free food.
"We only need 0.1% of that," the plan says. "That's $2 million a year." It sounds modest. It's almost certainly wrong.

image.label: A giant pie chart with a tiny sliver labeled 0.1%
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 거대한 파이 차트 위에 작은 조각 하나가 "0.1%" 라벨과 함께 빠져 있고, 그 조각을 빵집 주인 캐릭터가 들고 있음. 배경에 작은 동네 빵집. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Which estimate would you trust?
body: Your friend wants to open a gluten-free bakery in a mid-sized town and asks you to check the sales forecast before she signs a lease.
How should she estimate how much she could sell?

options.text: Take the national gluten-free market and assume a tiny share, like 0.1%
options.feedback: It's quick and sounds humble. But nothing tells her where the 0.1% comes from, so the number can't be checked or trusted.

options.text: Count nearby households that buy gluten-free, then multiply by what they spend
options.feedback: Slower, and every input is a guess. But each guess is something she can check by walking the town and talking to buyers.

options.text: Copy the sales of a successful gluten-free bakery in a big city
options.feedback: Real numbers help. But a big city has far more nearby buyers, so the result may still be far too high.

cards.title: The same bakery, counted one household at a time.
body: The whole local market is about **$624,000** a year. Even winning 30% of it, a big share for one shop, means about $187,000. Not $2 million.

cards.title: Sizing a market
body: **Sizing a market** means estimating how much the customers you can actually reach will spend in a year on the problem you solve.
There are two ways to do it. *Top-down* starts with a big industry figure and cuts it down. **Bottom-up** starts with real customers: how many there are, how often they buy, and what they pay.
Investors often call these layers TAM, SAM and SOM: the total market, the part you can serve, and the part you can realistically win.

image.label: Funnel narrowing from national market to reachable customers
image.brief: 깔때기 인포그래픽. 위에서부터 "Whole country", "Customers you can reach", "Customers you can win" 세 층. 맨 아래 층만 강조 색. 깔때기 옆에 작은 가구 아이콘들이 하나씩 세어지는 모습.

cards.title: Nobody buys a percentage.
body: The "1% of a huge market" pitch is common enough that many investors treat it as a warning sign. The problem isn't that 1% is too big. It's that the share comes from nowhere.
You never win a slice of a national market. You win customers one at a time, in places you can reach, against shops they already use.
Bottom-up math forces you to name those customers. That also shows you what to test first.

cards.title: A small market isn't always a bad one.
body: $187,000 may be plenty for one bakery with low rent. It would be far too small for a company trying to raise venture funding, which needs a path to many millions.
So the real question is whether the market is big enough for the business you want to build. Size also changes: a small market that is growing fast can matter more than a large, shrinking one.
cards.softwareNote: Software can reach customers anywhere, so the "15-minute drive" limit disappears. But the bottom-up rule stays: count the companies who have the problem, can find you, and will pay, instead of quoting the whole industry.

cards.title: Bottom-up numbers are guesses too.
body: Each input is an assumption, and errors multiply. If the 6% is really 3% and the $10 is really $5, the market is a quarter of the estimate.

So don't polish the spreadsheet. Find the shakiest number and check it: count shoppers, ask a local grocer what sells, or take pre-orders. For brand-new products with no history, treat any market size as a rough range, not a fact.

image.label: Stacked blocks with one wobbling block labeled 6%
image.brief: 쌓아 올린 블록 탑. 각 블록에 "20,000 households", "6%", "$10/week" 라벨. "6%" 블록만 흔들리며 물음표 표시. 간결한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Now you lead a team inside a software company.
body: Your company sells accounting software to 8,000 small businesses. A product team wants to build a payroll add-on. Their slide says payroll is a multi-billion-dollar industry.
Before approving a year of work, what estimate do you ask for?

options.text: How many of our 8,000 customers have staff, what they pay for payroll today, and how many would switch
options.feedback: It starts from users the team can actually reach. It takes some digging, but it shows quickly whether the add-on is worth a year.

options.text: Take the industry figure and apply a small share from an analyst report
options.feedback: It looks rigorous because it cites a report. But the share still says nothing about your own customers or why they'd switch.

options.text: Survey customers, then multiply the "yes, I'd buy it" answers by the price
options.feedback: It's bottom-up, which is good. But saying yes in a survey costs nothing, so stated interest usually overstates real purchases.

cards.title: Count customers, don't slice markets.
body: A market is only as big as the customers you can reach, multiplied by how often they buy and what they pay.
**Try it today:** estimate your own market bottom-up in three lines: who can reach you, how many of them buy, and what they spend in a year. Circle the number you're least sure of.
